title: Procedural rights and concrete interests
summary: A procedural right can relax some demands of immediacy and redressability when it protects the claimant’s concrete interest, but a bare procedural violation does not automatically confer standing.
notes:
A person accorded a procedural right to protect a concrete interest may challenge the failure to follow that procedure without proving that the procedure will certainly produce a different substantive outcome. The assigned Lujan footnote example concerns a resident beside a proposed dam who seeks the environmental analysis required before licensing. The claimant’s connection to the site supplies the concrete interest; the omitted procedure relates to protecting it.

Massachusetts v. EPA uses a procedural-right analysis in reviewing denial of a rulemaking petition. The casebook questions how far that reasoning extends because the cited Clean Air Act provision concerns judicial review and venue. It therefore does not treat every avenue of judicial review as automatically eliminating ordinary standing requirements.

Spokeo and TransUnion reinforce the independent need for concrete harm. A statutory procedure and authorization to sue are significant, but they do not entitle every person to federal adjudication merely because a procedure was violated. Analyze the actual interest, the connection between procedure and harm, and the remedy sought.
